title: Microbiology
summary: A full college microbiology course in syllabus order: cells, viruses, growth, control, genetics, drugs, infection, immunity, and the pathogens that show up on the exam and in the hospital.

lessons.title: Scope, microscopy and the logic of staining
lessons.body:
Microbiology is the study of organisms too small to see with the naked eye: bacteria, archaea, fungi, protozoa, algae, and the non-living infectious agents (viruses, viroids, prions). The whole field exists because of one instrument. If you cannot see them, you cannot count them, classify them, or prove they cause disease.

## The history the exam asks about

Antonie van Leeuwenhoek ground his own lenses in the 1670s and drew the first bacteria, which he called "animalcules." Louis Pasteur's swan-neck flask experiment (1861) killed spontaneous generation: broth in a flask with a curved neck stayed sterile for months because dust and microbes settled in the bend, but tipping the flask so broth touched the neck produced growth. Pasteur also gave us pasteurization and the germ theory of disease. Joseph Lister applied germ theory to surgery with phenol (carbolic acid) in 1867. Robert Koch gave us pure-culture technique and Koch's postulates. Edward Jenner used cowpox to protect against smallpox in 1796, and Alexander Fleming noticed a *Penicillium* mold clearing a *Staphylococcus* plate in 1928.

## Why things are the size they are

A typical bacterium is `0.2–2 micrometers` wide and `1–10 micrometers` long. A human red blood cell is about `7 micrometers`. A virus is `20–300 nanometers` — a thousand times smaller than the cell it infects. Those numbers set the tools: light microscopes for bacteria and eukaryotic microbes, electron microscopes for viruses.

A compound light microscope's total magnification is objective power times ocular power. The `100x` oil-immersion objective with a `10x` ocular gives `1000x`. Oil is not for magnification; it has the same refractive index as glass, so it keeps light rays from bending away and being lost. The practical resolution limit of light microscopy is about `0.2 micrometers`, which is exactly why viruses are invisible to it.

> **Key:** Magnification makes an image bigger. Resolution makes it clearer. Past `0.2 micrometers` a light microscope only gives you a bigger blur.

## Why we stain

Bacterial cytoplasm is mostly water and barely bends light, so unstained cells are nearly transparent. Dyes fix that. Basic dyes (crystal violet, methylene blue, safranin, malachite green) carry a positive charge and are attracted to the negatively charged bacterial surface — that is why almost every routine stain is a basic dye.

A **simple stain** uses one dye and shows shape and arrangement. A **differential stain** uses more than one and separates groups.

The **Gram stain** (Hans Christian Gram, 1884) is the first test run on almost any clinical specimen. Four steps: crystal violet (primary dye, stains everything purple), Gram's iodine (mordant, forms a large crystal violet–iodine complex), alcohol or acetone (decolorizer, the critical step), safranin (counterstain, pink). Thick peptidoglycan in Gram-positive walls traps the complex and the cells stay purple. Thin peptidoglycan behind an outer membrane that alcohol dissolves lets the complex wash out, so Gram-negative cells take up safranin and appear pink.

The **acid-fast stain** (Ziehl-Neelsen) exists for one genus problem: *Mycobacterium* and *Nocardia* have mycolic acid, a waxy lipid that repels water-based dyes. Carbolfuchsin is driven in with heat, then acid-alcohol is applied. Acid-fast cells hold the red dye; everything else decolorizes and takes the methylene blue counterstain.

> **Trap:** Over-decolorizing turns a Gram-positive organism pink. A culture older than `24 hours` also loses wall integrity and can read falsely Gram-negative. Always Gram stain a fresh culture.

Special stains handle structures the routine stains miss: the capsule stain is a negative stain (India ink) that leaves a clear halo because capsules do not take dye; the endospore stain uses malachite green plus heat with a safranin counterstain; the flagellar stain builds up mordant to thicken flagella enough to be seen.
keyPoints: Bacteria are 0.2–2 by 1–10 micrometers; viruses 20–300 nanometers; light microscopy resolves to about 0.2 micrometers.
Oil immersion matches the refractive index of glass so light is not lost; it improves resolution, not magnification.
Gram stain order: crystal violet, iodine mordant, alcohol decolorizer, safranin. Purple equals Gram-positive, pink equals Gram-negative.
Acid-fast stain detects mycolic acid in Mycobacterium and Nocardia; carbolfuchsin resists acid-alcohol.
Pasteur disproved spontaneous generation; Koch proved specific microbes cause specific diseases.

checks.q: Which step of the Gram stain actually determines the final result?
checks.why: Every cell is purple after crystal violet and iodine. Decolorization is what removes the dye complex from thin-walled Gram-negative cells, so timing errors here cause most false results.

checks.q: Why are viruses invisible under a standard light microscope?
choices: They do not take up basic dyes
They are smaller than the roughly 0.2 micrometer resolution limit
They are transparent to visible light only when alive
They require a mordant that destroys them
checks.why: Resolution, not magnification, is the limit. Viruses at 20–300 nanometers fall below 0.2 micrometers, so electron microscopy is required regardless of staining.

checks.q: A student reads a Gram-positive Staphylococcus culture as Gram-negative. The culture was incubated 48 hours. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: Old cells lose cell wall integrity and decolorize
checks.why: Aging cultures lyse and thin their peptidoglycan, so they over-decolorize. Gram reaction is a wall property, not a mutation; omitting safranin would leave cells colorless, not pink.

lessons.title: Prokaryotic cell structure
lessons.body:
Prokaryote means "before nucleus." Bacteria and archaea have no nuclear membrane, no mitochondria, no endoplasmic reticulum, and no Golgi. Their DNA sits in an irregular region called the nucleoid. Everything the exam tests about prokaryotes comes down to structures outside the cytoplasm, because those structures are what our drugs attack and what our immune system sees.

## Shape and arrangement

Three basic shapes: **coccus** (sphere), **bacillus** (rod), **spiral** (vibrio is a comma, spirillum is rigid, spirochete is flexible). Arrangement follows the plane of division. Diplo- means pairs, strepto- means chains, staphylo- means clusters. *Streptococcus pyogenes* is a chain of spheres; *Staphylococcus aureus* is a cluster.

## The cell wall

The wall is made of **peptidoglycan** (murein): alternating sugars N-acetylglucosamine (NAG) and N-acetylmuramic acid (NAM) cross-linked by short peptide bridges. It exists to resist osmotic pressure. A bacterium in a hypotonic environment would burst without it.

**Gram-positive walls** are `20–80 nanometers` of thick peptidoglycan with **teichoic acids** woven through. Teichoic acids give negative charge, bind cations, and are antigenic.

**Gram-negative walls** are `2–7 nanometers` of thin peptidoglycan plus an **outer membrane** containing **lipopolysaccharide (LPS)**. LPS has three parts: O antigen (used for serotyping, as in *E. coli* O157:H7), core polysaccharide, and **lipid A**. Lipid A is endotoxin. It is released when the cell dies and triggers fever, vasodilation, hypotension and disseminated intravascular coagulation. Between the membranes sits the periplasmic space, where beta-lactamase enzymes concentrate. Porins in the outer membrane control what gets in, which is one reason Gram-negatives are intrinsically harder to kill.

> **Key:** Penicillin blocks cross-linking of peptidoglycan. Lysozyme in tears and saliva cuts the NAG–NAM bond. Both work better on Gram-positives because there is no outer membrane in the way.

*Mycoplasma* has no cell wall at all — it is the exception, and it is why beta-lactams never work for *Mycoplasma pneumoniae*.

## Outside the wall

The **glycocalyx** is a sugar coat. When it is organized and firmly attached it is a **capsule**; when loose it is a **slime layer**. Capsules block phagocytosis, which is why *Streptococcus pneumoniae* and *Klebsiella pneumoniae* are dangerous and why their vaccines target capsular polysaccharide. Slime layers anchor **biofilms** on catheters, heart valves and prosthetic joints.

**Flagella** provide motility by rotating like a propeller, driven by proton motive force. Monotrichous is one flagellum, lophotrichous is a tuft, amphitrichous is both ends, peritrichous is all over. Movement toward a chemical gradient is **chemotaxis**: runs and tumbles, with fewer tumbles when conditions improve. The H antigen is flagellar protein.

**Fimbriae** are short and numerous and their job is adhesion — *Neisseria gonorrhoeae* cannot cause disease without them. A **pilus** (sex pilus) is longer, usually one or two per cell, and transfers DNA during conjugation. Do not confuse the two.

## Inside

Ribosomes are **70S** (30S + 50S subunits), versus 80S in eukaryotes. That difference is the entire basis of selective toxicity for aminoglycosides, tetracyclines, macrolides and clindamycin.

The chromosome is a single circular double-stranded DNA molecule. **Plasmids** are small circular extras that are not required for survival but often carry resistance genes (R factors), toxin genes or conjugation machinery.

**Endospores** are dormant survival structures made by *Bacillus* and *Clostridium* (both Gram-positive rods). Sporulation is triggered by nutrient depletion. The core is dehydrated and packed with calcium dipicolinate and small acid-soluble proteins, so spores survive boiling, drying, radiation and most disinfectants. Killing them requires an autoclave at `121 degrees Celsius, 15 psi, for 15 minutes`.

> **On the exam:** "Not killed by boiling" always means endospore. "Fever and shock after a Gram-negative bacteremia" always means lipid A endotoxin.
keyPoints: Peptidoglycan is NAG–NAM with peptide cross-links; thick with teichoic acid in Gram-positives, thin plus an outer membrane in Gram-negatives.
Lipid A of LPS is endotoxin — fever, hypotension, shock — and is released when Gram-negatives die.
Capsules block phagocytosis; fimbriae adhere; sex pili transfer DNA; flagella move the cell.
Bacterial ribosomes are 70S versus 80S in humans, which is why protein-synthesis inhibitors are selectively toxic.
Endospores from Bacillus and Clostridium survive boiling; autoclave 121 degrees Celsius at 15 psi for 15 minutes.

checks.q: A patient with Gram-negative bacteremia spikes a fever and drops her blood pressure shortly after antibiotics are started. What explains this?
choices: Lipid A released from lysed cell walls
checks.why: Lipid A is endotoxin, part of the Gram-negative outer membrane, released on lysis — which antibiotics cause. Exotoxins are actively secreted proteins; teichoic acid is a Gram-positive structure.

checks.q: Why do beta-lactams fail against Mycoplasma pneumoniae?
choices: It has an unusually thick capsule
It has no peptidoglycan cell wall
It lives only inside host cells
checks.why: Mycoplasma lacks a cell wall entirely, so there is no peptidoglycan cross-linking for a beta-lactam to inhibit. Treatment uses macrolides, tetracyclines or fluoroquinolones.

checks.q: Which structure is responsible for the ability of Streptococcus pneumoniae to evade phagocytosis?
checks.why: The capsule is slippery and hides surface antigens from phagocytes. Fimbriae mediate attachment, not evasion, and S. pneumoniae is non-motile and does not form spores.

lessons.title: Eukaryotic microbes: fungi, protozoa and helminths
lessons.body:
Eukaryotic microbes have a true nucleus, membrane-bound organelles, 80S ribosomes and sterols in their membranes. That last detail matters clinically: because their cells look a lot like ours, antifungal and antiparasitic drugs are far more toxic to the patient than antibacterials are.

## Fungi

Fungi are chemoheterotrophs that absorb nutrients after secreting digestive enzymes. Their cell wall is **chitin**, not peptidoglycan, and their membranes use **ergosterol** where ours use cholesterol. Ergosterol is the target of the azoles (which block its synthesis) and amphotericin B (which binds it and punches pores).

Two body plans. **Yeasts** are single cells that reproduce by budding; *Candida albicans* and *Cryptococcus neoformans* are yeasts. **Molds** grow as filaments called **hyphae** that form a visible mat called a **mycelium**; septate hyphae have cross-walls, coenocytic hyphae do not. **Dimorphic** fungi switch: mold at `25 degrees Celsius` in the environment, yeast at `37 degrees Celsius` in the body. *Histoplasma*, *Blastomyces*, *Coccidioides* and *Sporothrix* are the classic dimorphs.

Reproduction can be asexual (conidiospores, sporangiospores) or sexual (ascospores, basidiospores, zygospores), and that is how mycologists classify them.

Clinical categories: **superficial and cutaneous** (dermatophytes causing tinea — ringworm, athlete's foot, jock itch), **subcutaneous** (sporotrichosis, the "rose gardener's disease"), **systemic** (histoplasmosis from bird and bat droppings in the Ohio and Mississippi valleys, coccidioidomycosis or Valley fever in the southwestern deserts), and **opportunistic** (*Candida*, *Aspergillus*, *Pneumocystis jirovecii*, *Cryptococcus*) which strike only the immunocompromised.

> **On shift:** Oral thrush in an adult with no obvious cause is a reason to think about HIV, inhaled steroids, or recent broad-spectrum antibiotics that wiped out competing flora.

## Protozoa

Protozoa are single-celled animal-like eukaryotes. Many alternate between a motile feeding **trophozoite** and a hardy **cyst** that survives outside the host and transmits infection. Chlorination does not reliably kill *Giardia* or *Cryptosporidium* cysts — filtration does.

Classify by motility. **Amoebas** move with pseudopods: *Entamoeba histolytica* causes bloody amebic dysentery and liver abscess. **Flagellates** move with flagella: *Giardia lamblia* (greasy, foul diarrhea from streams or daycare), *Trichomonas vaginalis* (frothy green-yellow discharge, sexually transmitted, no cyst stage), *Trypanosoma* (African sleeping sickness, Chagas disease). **Ciliates**: *Balantidium coli*. **Apicomplexans** are non-motile intracellular parasites: *Plasmodium* (malaria, spread by the female *Anopheles* mosquito), *Toxoplasma gondii* (cat feces and undercooked meat; a major threat in pregnancy and in AIDS), *Cryptosporidium* (watery diarrhea, chlorine-resistant, a pool outbreak classic).

## Helminths

Helminths are multicellular worms, not microbes at all, but the micro course teaches them because they are infectious agents. They are diagnosed by finding eggs (ova) or larvae in stool.

**Nematodes** (roundworms) include *Ascaris lumbricoides*, hookworm (*Necator*, larvae penetrate bare feet and cause iron-deficiency anemia), *Enterobius vermicularis* (pinworm, perianal itching at night, diagnosed with the cellophane tape test), and *Trichinella spiralis* from undercooked pork. **Cestodes** (tapeworms) are flat and segmented: *Taenia saginata* from beef, *Taenia solium* from pork (whose eggs can cause neurocysticercosis). **Trematodes** (flukes) are leaf-shaped: *Schistosoma* penetrates skin in fresh water.

Helminth infections classically raise the **eosinophil** count — a peripheral eosinophilia on a CBC in a traveler is a parasite until proven otherwise.

> **Trap:** "Fungal" does not mean "harmless." *Cryptococcus neoformans* meningitis and invasive aspergillosis both kill, and the antifungals used against them (amphotericin B, "ampho-terrible") cause real nephrotoxicity.
keyPoints: Fungal walls are chitin and membranes use ergosterol — the target of azoles and amphotericin B.
Dimorphic fungi are mold at 25 degrees Celsius and yeast at 37 degrees Celsius: Histoplasma, Blastomyces, Coccidioides, Sporothrix.
Protozoan cysts survive outside the host; Giardia and Cryptosporidium resist chlorination and require filtration.
Apicomplexans include Plasmodium, Toxoplasma and Cryptosporidium; Plasmodium is spread by the female Anopheles mosquito.
Helminth infection typically causes eosinophilia and is diagnosed by ova and parasites in stool.

checks.q: A culture grown at 25 degrees Celsius shows filamentous mold; the same organism at 37 degrees Celsius grows as budding yeast. This organism is best described as:
checks.why: Temperature-dependent switching between mold and yeast forms defines dimorphism. Coenocytic describes hyphae without septa, and saprophytic describes feeding on dead matter.

checks.q: A municipal pool outbreak causes weeks of watery diarrhea despite normal chlorination. Most likely agent?
checks.why: Cryptosporidium oocysts are chlorine-resistant and cause prolonged watery diarrhea; filtration is required. Entamoeba causes bloody dysentery, Trichomonas is sexually transmitted, and Taenia comes from undercooked pork.

checks.q: Why are antifungal drugs generally more toxic to humans than antibacterial drugs?
choices: Fungi are eukaryotes with cell machinery similar to ours
checks.why: Selective toxicity depends on differences between pathogen and host. Fungi are eukaryotes, so fewer unique targets exist; peptidoglycan and 70S ribosomes are bacterial features.

lessons.title: Viruses, replication cycles and prions
lessons.body:
A virus is an obligate intracellular parasite: a nucleic acid genome in a protein coat with no metabolism, no ribosomes, and no ability to make ATP. Outside a cell it is an inert particle. That is why we call it an agent rather than an organism, and why antibiotics do nothing to it.

## Structure

The genome is **either DNA or RNA, never both**, and can be single- or double-stranded, linear or circular, segmented or not. The protein coat is the **capsid**, built from repeating subunits called **capsomeres**; genome plus capsid is the **nucleocapsid**. Capsid symmetry is helical, icosahedral, or complex (bacteriophages and poxviruses).

Some viruses wrap themselves in host membrane on the way out — these are **enveloped**, and the envelope carries virus-coded **spikes** (influenza hemagglutinin and neuraminidase, SARS-CoV-2 spike, HIV gp120). Envelopes are lipid, so alcohol, soap and detergents destroy them easily. **Naked** (non-enveloped) viruses have only a protein capsid and are far more resistant to drying and disinfectants — norovirus and hepatitis A survive on surfaces and in food, which is why they cause outbreaks.

> **Key:** Enveloped equals fragile and usually needs close contact or body fluids. Naked equals tough and spreads through surfaces, water and food.

Host range is set by the fit between viral attachment protein and host cell receptor. HIV gp120 binds CD4 plus a co-receptor (CCR5 or CXCR4), which is why it destroys helper T cells specifically. Rabies binds acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction.

## The five steps of animal virus replication

1. **Attachment** to a specific receptor.
2. **Penetration and uncoating** — enveloped viruses fuse with the membrane or enter by endocytosis; the capsid then comes apart.
3. **Biosynthesis** — the genome directs synthesis of viral proteins and copies of the genome using host ribosomes.
4. **Assembly (maturation)** of new virions.
5. **Release** — naked viruses generally lyse the cell; enveloped viruses **bud**, taking membrane with them, which can let the cell survive and keep producing virus.

## Lytic versus lysogenic

Bacteriophages make the distinction cleanest. In the **lytic cycle** the phage attaches, injects its DNA, takes over, assembles new phage and bursts the cell — five steps: attachment, penetration, biosynthesis, maturation, lysis. In the **lysogenic cycle** the phage DNA integrates into the bacterial chromosome as a **prophage** and is copied every time the cell divides. The cell is unharmed until an inducing event (UV light, stress) triggers the switch to lytic.

Lysogeny matters because of **lysogenic conversion**: the prophage gives the bacterium new properties. Diphtheria toxin, botulinum toxin, cholera toxin, scarlet fever erythrogenic toxin and Shiga toxin in *E. coli* O157:H7 are all phage-encoded. A harmless organism becomes a killer because a virus moved in. The animal-cell equivalent is **latency**: herpesviruses (HSV-1 in the trigeminal ganglion, varicella-zoster in dorsal root ganglia reactivating as shingles) and HIV provirus.

## Retroviruses and oncogenic viruses

**Retroviruses** carry `+ssRNA` plus **reverse transcriptase**, which makes DNA from RNA — backwards from the central dogma. **Integrase** then inserts that DNA into the host chromosome as a provirus, permanently. HIV and HTLV-1 are the human examples, and reverse transcriptase, integrase and protease are each drug targets.

Oncogenic viruses cause cancer by inserting genes that disrupt growth control: HPV types 16 and 18 (cervical cancer), hepatitis B and C (hepatocellular carcinoma), Epstein-Barr virus (Burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma), HTLV-1, and HHV-8 (Kaposi sarcoma).

Viruses are grown in embryonated eggs, live animals, or **cell culture**, where damage called **cytopathic effect (CPE)** — inclusion bodies, syncytia, rounding — is how you know infection took. Quantification uses the plaque assay, reported in plaque-forming units.

## Subviral agents

**Viroids** are naked short RNA circles that infect plants. **Prions** are the strange ones: infectious **proteins** with no nucleic acid at all. A misfolded PrP-Sc protein converts normal PrP-C into the misfolded form, which accumulates and produces spongy holes in the brain. Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, variant CJD from bovine spongiform encephalopathy, kuru and scrapie are prion diseases. They resist autoclaving, formalin and radiation, and instrument decontamination requires extended autoclaving with `1 N sodium hydroxide`.

> **Trap:** Prions are not killed by standard sterilization. This is the classic "which agent survives the autoclave" exam item, alongside endospores.
keyPoints: A virus has DNA or RNA, never both, plus a capsid; enveloped viruses are fragile, naked viruses resist drying and disinfectants.
Animal replication: attachment, penetration and uncoating, biosynthesis, assembly, release by lysis or budding.
Lysogenic conversion via prophage gives bacteria toxin genes — diphtheria, botulinum, cholera, Shiga.
Retroviruses use reverse transcriptase and integrase to place a permanent DNA provirus in the host genome.
Prions are infectious misfolded proteins with no nucleic acid and survive standard autoclaving.

checks.q: A nonpathogenic Corynebacterium strain begins producing diphtheria toxin after phage infection. This is an example of:
checks.why: A prophage integrated into the chromosome supplies the toxin gene, changing the phenotype — that is lysogenic conversion. Transformation is uptake of naked DNA, and reverse transcription is a retroviral step.

checks.q: Norovirus spreads easily through contaminated surfaces and survives alcohol hand rubs. Which structural feature explains this?
choices: It is a naked virus with only a protein capsid
checks.why: Lipid envelopes are dissolved by alcohol and detergents; naked capsids are not, so they persist on surfaces. Capsid symmetry and reverse transcriptase do not determine environmental resistance.

checks.q: Which enzyme is unique to retroviruses and makes DNA from an RNA template?
checks.why: Reverse transcriptase makes DNA from RNA. Integrase then inserts that DNA, and protease cleaves polyproteins — both are retroviral but neither reverses the flow of information.

lessons.title: Microbial growth, metabolism and culture
lessons.body:
"Growth" in microbiology means an increase in the number of cells, not the size of one cell. Bacteria divide by **binary fission**, so growth is exponential: one cell becomes 2, 4, 8, 16. The **generation time** is how long a doubling takes — `20 minutes` for *E. coli* under ideal conditions, `15–20 hours` for *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*, which is why TB cultures take up to `6–8 weeks` and TB treatment lasts `6–9 months`.

The number of cells after n generations is starting number times `2^n`. Start with 100 cells and let *E. coli* grow `3 hours` at a 20-minute generation time: that is 9 generations, `100 x 2^9 = 51,200` cells.

## The growth curve

Four phases in a closed batch culture:

- **Lag** — no division; cells are making enzymes and ribosomes and adapting.
- **Log (exponential)** — constant maximum doubling. Cells are most metabolically active and **most susceptible to antibiotics**, because penicillin needs cells actively building wall.
- **Stationary** — new cells equal dying cells as nutrients run out and waste accumulates. Endospores form here, and so do many exotoxins.
- **Death (decline)** — exponential dying.

> **Trap:** Antibiotics that target the cell wall do almost nothing to bacteria that are not dividing. That is part of why abscesses and biofilms fail medical therapy and need drainage.

## Physical requirements

**Temperature.** Psychrophiles grow in cold, mesophiles at `25–40 degrees Celsius` (nearly every human pathogen, optimum `37 degrees Celsius`), thermophiles at `50–60 degrees Celsius`, hyperthermophiles above `80 degrees Celsius`. *Listeria monocytogenes* is the exception that matters: it grows at refrigerator temperature, so deli meats and soft cheeses transmit it.

**pH.** Most pathogens are neutrophiles, pH `6.5–7.5`. Molds and yeasts tolerate acid down to pH `5`. *Helicobacter pylori* survives stomach acid by making urease, which splits urea into ammonia and buffers its microenvironment — that is also the basis of the urea breath test.

**Osmotic pressure.** High salt or sugar pulls water out of cells (plasmolysis), which is why salting and candying preserve food. **Halophiles** need salt; *Staphylococcus aureus* is halotolerant up to `7.5%` NaCl, which is what mannitol salt agar exploits.

## Oxygen

- **Obligate aerobe** — needs O2 (*Mycobacterium tuberculosis*, *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*).
- **Obligate anaerobe** — killed by O2 (*Clostridium*, *Bacteroides*).
- **Facultative anaerobe** — uses O2 when present, ferments when not (*E. coli*, *Staphylococcus*). Most clinical isolates.
- **Aerotolerant anaerobe** — ignores O2, never uses it (*Lactobacillus*).
- **Microaerophile** — needs low O2, `2–10%` (*Campylobacter*, *Helicobacter*).

Oxygen is toxic because metabolism generates superoxide and hydrogen peroxide. Aerobes survive by making **superoxide dismutase** and **catalase**; anaerobes lack them. The catalase test (bubbles in hydrogen peroxide) separates *Staphylococcus* (catalase positive) from *Streptococcus* (negative).

## Energy metabolism

**Aerobic respiration** oxidizes glucose completely, using O2 as the final electron acceptor, and nets about `38 ATP` in prokaryotes. **Anaerobic respiration** uses an inorganic acceptor such as nitrate or sulfate and yields less. **Fermentation** uses an organic molecule as the final electron acceptor, regenerates NAD+, and nets only `2 ATP` — but it is fast and it produces the acids and gases that identification tests read: lactic acid, ethanol and CO2, mixed acids, or 2,3-butanediol.

## Culture media

- **Chemically defined** — exact composition known.
- **Complex** — extracts and digests (nutrient broth, tryptic soy).
- **Selective** — inhibits unwanted organisms (MacConkey with bile salts and crystal violet grows only Gram-negatives; mannitol salt at `7.5%` NaCl selects staphylococci).
- **Differential** — makes colonies look different (blood agar shows beta, alpha or gamma hemolysis; MacConkey turns lactose fermenters pink).
- **Enrichment** — favors a small population so it can be detected.

Anaerobes are grown in reducing media with sodium thioglycolate, in anaerobic jars, or in anaerobic chambers.

## Counting

**Direct plate count (serial dilution)** reports **colony-forming units per milliliter**; a countable plate has `25–250` colonies, and CFU/mL equals colonies divided by (dilution factor times volume plated). **Direct microscopic count** counts everything, alive or dead. **Turbidity** by spectrophotometer is fast and indirect. **Most probable number** is a statistical method for water testing.
keyPoints: Growth is exponential: N = N0 times 2^n. E. coli doubles in about 20 minutes, M. tuberculosis in 15–20 hours.
Log phase cells are most susceptible to antibiotics; stationary phase makes spores and many toxins.
Oxygen classes: obligate aerobe, obligate anaerobe, facultative anaerobe, aerotolerant, microaerophile; catalase and superoxide dismutase are the survival enzymes.
Aerobic respiration nets about 38 ATP; fermentation nets 2 ATP but regenerates NAD+ and produces the acids used for identification.
Plate counts report CFU/mL from plates with 25–250 colonies; MacConkey is selective and differential.

checks.q: A culture of 500 cells with a 30-minute generation time is incubated for 3 hours. How many cells are present?
checks.why: Three hours at 30 minutes per generation is 6 generations: 500 times 2^6 equals 500 times 64 equals 32,000. Multiplying by 6 instead of 2^6 gives the wrong 3,000.

checks.q: Why is penicillin least effective against bacteria in stationary phase?
choices: Stationary cells pump the drug out
Penicillin requires active peptidoglycan synthesis to act
Penicillin is inactivated at stationary pH
checks.why: Beta-lactams block cross-linking during wall construction, so a cell that is not building wall is largely spared. Efflux and ribosome changes are unrelated mechanisms.

checks.q: A plate from a 1:10,000 dilution with 0.1 mL plated yields 60 colonies. What is the original concentration?
checks.why: CFU/mL equals 60 divided by (10^-4 times 0.1) equals 60 divided by 10^-5 equals 6.0 x 10^6. Forgetting the 0.1 mL volume gives the incorrect 6.0 x 10^5.

lessons.title: Control of microbial growth: sterilization, disinfection, antisepsis
lessons.body:
Hospitals use these words precisely, and the exam tests the definitions before it tests anything else.

- **Sterilization** — destruction of *all* microbial life, including endospores. Absolute. No such thing as "mostly sterile."
- **Disinfection** — killing or removing pathogens from an inanimate object. Does not necessarily kill spores.
- **Antisepsis** — the same process on living tissue.
- **Sanitization** — reducing microbial counts to a safe public-health level, as in restaurant dishwashing.
- **Degerming** — mechanical removal, such as the alcohol swab before an injection.
- **-cide** kills (bactericide, virucide, sporicide, fungicide). **-static** inhibits growth without killing (bacteriostatic). A static agent depends on the host immune system to finish the job.

> **Key:** Sterilize instruments. Disinfect surfaces. Apply antiseptics to skin. Using the wrong verb on the exam is the fastest way to miss a question.

## How killing actually works

Antimicrobial agents work by damaging the plasma membrane, denaturing proteins, or damaging nucleic acids. Microbial death is **logarithmic** — a constant fraction dies per unit time, not a constant number. That is why the amount of time matters and why heavier organic loads (blood, feces, pus) require longer contact times.

Effectiveness depends on the number of microbes present, their type (spores and mycobacteria are hardest), the environment (organic matter, pH, temperature), the concentration of agent, and **contact time**.

Resistance order, easiest to hardest: enveloped viruses, Gram-positive bacteria, Gram-negative bacteria, fungi, naked viruses, mycobacteria, endospores, prions.

## Physical methods

**Moist heat** kills by denaturing protein and is far more efficient than dry heat. Boiling at `100 degrees Celsius` for `10 minutes` kills vegetative cells and most viruses but **not endospores**. The **autoclave** uses steam under pressure: `121 degrees Celsius` at `15 psi` for `15 minutes` at the point of contact. Steam must touch every surface, so overpacked loads and trapped air cause failures. Confirm with a biological indicator — spores of *Geobacillus stearothermophilus*.

**Pasteurization** is not sterilization. Classic batch is `63 degrees Celsius for 30 minutes`; high-temperature short-time is `72 degrees Celsius for 15 seconds`; ultra-high temperature is `140 degrees Celsius for 3 seconds` and does produce a sterile product.

**Dry heat** needs `170 degrees Celsius for 2 hours` in a hot-air oven; incineration is the most complete method of all.

**Filtration** removes microbes from heat-sensitive liquids such as vaccines and antibiotics. A `0.22 micrometer` membrane filter retains bacteria; HEPA filters air in operating rooms and airborne-isolation rooms.

**Cold** is bacteriostatic, not bactericidal — refrigeration slows growth, freezing preserves organisms. **Desiccation**, **osmotic pressure** (salting, sugaring) and **lyophilization** inhibit rather than kill.

**Radiation.** Ionizing radiation (gamma, X-ray, electron beam) penetrates deeply and is used for disposable plastics, sutures and some foods. Nonionizing UV at `260 nanometers` forms thymine dimers in DNA but does not penetrate glass, plastic or dirt — it is surface and air decontamination only.

## Chemical methods

- **Alcohols** — `60–90%` ethanol or isopropanol; denature protein and dissolve lipids. Need water to work, so `70%` beats `100%`. Not sporicidal. The basis of hand rubs.
- **Chlorine** — household bleach diluted `1:10` for blood spills; forms hypochlorous acid. Inactivated by organic matter.
- **Iodophors** — povidone-iodine, a skin antiseptic; needs `2 minutes` of dry time.
- **Chlorhexidine** — binds to skin and keeps killing for hours; standard for surgical scrub and central-line insertion, usually as `2%` chlorhexidine in `70%` alcohol.
- **Hydrogen peroxide** — poor on skin because human catalase destroys it; excellent for surfaces, and vaporized H2O2 sterilizes rooms.
- **Glutaraldehyde** at `2%` is a chemical sterilant for endoscopes at `10 hours`. **Ortho-phthalaldehyde** is its faster replacement.
- **Ethylene oxide gas** sterilizes heat-sensitive equipment but takes hours and is a carcinogen.
- **Quaternary ammonium compounds (quats)** — safe, common surface disinfectants, but weak against *Pseudomonas* and non-sporicidal.
- **Phenolics** — stable in organic matter, used in laboratory and hospital surface disinfection.

> **On shift:** Alcohol foam is the default for hand hygiene, but it does **not** kill *Clostridioides difficile* spores or norovirus. Those require soap and water plus physical friction, and the room gets bleach.
keyPoints: Sterilization kills everything including spores; disinfection is for objects; antisepsis is for living tissue.
Autoclave: 121 degrees Celsius, 15 psi, 15 minutes, verified with Geobacillus stearothermophilus spores.
70% alcohol beats 100% because water is required for protein denaturation; alcohol is not sporicidal.
UV at 260 nanometers makes thymine dimers but does not penetrate glass, plastic or soil.
C. difficile and norovirus require soap-and-water handwashing and bleach, not alcohol foam.

checks.q: An instrument is soaked in 70% alcohol for 20 minutes. Which claim is accurate?
choices: It is disinfected but not sterile because spores survive
checks.why: Alcohol is not sporicidal, so sterility cannot be claimed. Sanitization refers to reducing counts to a public-health standard and degerming refers to mechanical removal from skin.

checks.q: Why is 70% alcohol more effective than 95% alcohol?
choices: Water is needed to denature proteins
It has a lower flash point
It evaporates more slowly, increasing contact time only
checks.why: Protein denaturation requires water; absolute alcohol dehydrates the surface and coagulates it without penetrating. Alcohol never kills spores at any concentration.

checks.q: A patient has C. difficile colitis. Which hand hygiene is required after contact?
checks.why: C. difficile forms endospores that alcohol does not kill; friction with soap and water physically removes them. Chemical antiseptics alone do not solve a spore problem.

lessons.title: Microbial genetics and how resistance spreads
lessons.body:
Bacteria evolve fast for two reasons: they divide in minutes, and they trade genes sideways with unrelated organisms. Understanding both is understanding antibiotic resistance.

## The basics

The **genotype** is the genetic makeup; the **phenotype** is what is expressed. Bacterial DNA replication is bidirectional from a single origin and is semiconservative. Transcription makes mRNA, and because prokaryotes have no nucleus, translation begins while transcription is still going. Genes for one pathway sit together in an **operon** controlled by one promoter — the *lac* operon (inducible, off until lactose appears) and the *trp* operon (repressible, on until tryptophan accumulates) are the two every course covers.

## Mutation

A **mutation** is a permanent change in the base sequence. **Point mutation** (base substitution) can be **silent** (same amino acid), **missense** (different amino acid), or **nonsense** (premature stop). **Frameshift** mutations from insertion or deletion of bases not in multiples of three scramble everything downstream and are usually devastating.

Spontaneous mutation rate is roughly `1 in 10^9` per base per replication — vanishingly small per cell, but a single colony contains `10^9` cells, so mutants are always present. Mutagens raise the rate: chemical mutagens such as nitrous acid and base analogs, and radiation (X-rays cause breaks; UV causes thymine dimers).

The **Ames test** uses a histidine-requiring *Salmonella* strain to screen chemicals for mutagenicity — reversion to growth without histidine means the chemical is a mutagen, and mutagens correlate with carcinogens.

> **Key:** Antibiotics do not create resistance. They kill the susceptible majority and leave the rare pre-existing mutant to repopulate. That is selection, not induction.

## Horizontal gene transfer

Vertical transfer is parent to offspring. **Horizontal** transfer moves genes between existing cells, even across species, and is why resistance spreads faster than mutation alone can explain. Three mechanisms:

**Transformation** — the cell takes up naked DNA released from a dead neighbor. The cell must be **competent**. Griffith showed this in 1928 with *Streptococcus pneumoniae*: heat-killed virulent S strain plus live harmless R strain killed mice, because the R strain absorbed the capsule gene. Avery, MacLeod and McCarty later proved the transforming substance was DNA.

**Transduction** — bacteriophage carries bacterial DNA from one cell to another. **Generalized** transduction packages any random fragment during lytic assembly; **specialized** transduction moves genes adjacent to the prophage site when it excises imprecisely.

**Conjugation** — direct transfer through a **sex pilus** encoded by the F plasmid. F+ donor transfers a copy of the plasmid to an F- recipient, making it F+. An Hfr cell has the F factor integrated into the chromosome and transfers chromosomal genes. Conjugation moves **R plasmids**, which frequently carry several resistance genes at once, so one transfer event can create a multidrug-resistant organism.

**Transposons** ("jumping genes") move within and between DNA molecules, carrying resistance genes onto plasmids that then conjugate. **Integrons** collect gene cassettes the same way.

## Resistance mechanisms

Five to memorize:

1. **Enzymatic destruction or modification** — beta-lactamases hydrolyze the beta-lactam ring; extended-spectrum beta-lactamases (ESBL) defeat third-generation cephalosporins; carbapenemases (KPC, NDM) defeat carbapenems; aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes acetylate or phosphorylate the drug.
2. **Target alteration** — MRSA's *mecA* gene makes PBP2a, a penicillin-binding protein beta-lactams cannot bind, which makes the organism resistant to every beta-lactam at once. VRE alters the peptidoglycan terminus from D-Ala-D-Ala to D-Ala-D-Lac so vancomycin cannot bind. Ribosomal methylation blocks macrolides.
3. **Decreased permeability** — porin loss in *Pseudomonas* and *Acinetobacter*.
4. **Efflux pumps** — actively export the drug, often several classes at once.
5. **Bypass or overproduction of the target** — extra PABA overwhelming sulfonamides.

> **On shift:** Every course of antibiotics selects resistance somewhere in the patient's flora. That is the whole argument behind antibiotic stewardship, narrow-spectrum choices, and not treating viral upper respiratory infections.
keyPoints: Mutation types: silent, missense, nonsense, frameshift; spontaneous rate about 1 in 10^9 per base per replication.
Transformation takes up naked DNA, transduction uses a phage vector, conjugation uses a sex pilus and an F or R plasmid.
R plasmids and transposons move multiple resistance genes at once, creating multidrug resistance in a single event.
MRSA resistance is mecA producing PBP2a; VRE changes D-Ala-D-Ala to D-Ala-D-Lac.
Antibiotics select for pre-existing resistant mutants rather than causing the mutation.

checks.q: An E. coli isolate acquires resistance to ampicillin, gentamicin and sulfonamide simultaneously after contact with a Klebsiella isolate. Most likely mechanism?
choices: Conjugative transfer of an R plasmid
Frameshift mutation in a porin gene
checks.why: Simultaneous multidrug resistance across species points to a conjugative R plasmid carrying several genes. A point or frameshift mutation would affect one target, and transduction is far less efficient for this pattern.

checks.q: MRSA is resistant to all beta-lactams because mecA encodes:
checks.why: PBP2a still builds cell wall but has low affinity for beta-lactams, so the entire class fails. Beta-lactamase alone is defeated by a beta-lactamase inhibitor, which is why the distinction matters.

checks.q: The Ames test detects a chemical's potential to be:
checks.why: Reversion of a histidine-auxotroph Salmonella to growth without histidine indicates mutation, and mutagenicity correlates strongly with carcinogenicity. The test measures mutation, not killing.

lessons.title: Antimicrobial drugs: classes, mechanisms and testing
lessons.body:
The governing principle is **selective toxicity**: harm the microbe more than the host. It works best when the drug hits a target that exists in the pathogen and not in us — peptidoglycan, 70S ribosomes, bacterial folate synthesis, DNA gyrase.

**Spectrum** describes range. Narrow-spectrum drugs hit a limited group; broad-spectrum drugs hit many, which sounds better but wipes out normal flora and invites **superinfection** — *C. difficile* colitis and *Candida* overgrowth are the classic consequences.

Drugs are **bactericidal** (kill) or **bacteriostatic** (stop growth, leaving the immune system to clear). In a neutropenic patient or in endocarditis and meningitis, you want cidal.

## Cell wall inhibitors (bactericidal)

**Beta-lactams** share a beta-lactam ring and bind penicillin-binding proteins, blocking peptidoglycan cross-linking.

- Penicillins: natural penicillin G and V (narrow, Gram-positive, *Streptococcus*, syphilis); antistaphylococcal nafcillin and oxacillin (beta-lactamase resistant); aminopenicillins amoxicillin and ampicillin (extended to some Gram-negatives); piperacillin (antipseudomonal).
- Beta-lactamase inhibitor combinations: amoxicillin-clavulanate, piperacillin-tazobactam. The inhibitor has almost no antibacterial activity itself; it protects the partner drug.
- Cephalosporins by generation, gaining Gram-negative coverage and losing Gram-positive as you go up: first (cefazolin, surgical prophylaxis), second (cefuroxime), third (ceftriaxone, crosses into CSF — the meningitis and gonorrhea drug), fourth (cefepime), fifth (ceftaroline, covers MRSA).
- Carbapenems (meropenem, ertapenem) are the broadest, reserved for resistant Gram-negatives. Monobactam aztreonam is Gram-negative only and safe in severe penicillin allergy.

**Vancomycin** is a glycopeptide that binds the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus rather than an enzyme. Gram-positive only — it cannot cross the Gram-negative outer membrane. It is the MRSA workhorse, requires level monitoring, and causes "red man syndrome" if infused too quickly (a histamine reaction, not an allergy).

## Protein synthesis inhibitors (70S target)

- **30S**: aminoglycosides (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin) are bactericidal, aerobic Gram-negative coverage, with nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity that require trough monitoring. Tetracyclines and doxycycline are static, broad, cover atypicals and tick-borne illness, chelate calcium, and are avoided in pregnancy and in children under `8 years`.
- **50S**: macrolides (azithromycin, erythromycin) cover atypical pneumonia and prolong the QT interval; clindamycin covers anaerobes above the diaphragm and carries the strongest *C. difficile* association; linezolid (oxazolidinone) covers MRSA and VRE; chloramphenicol causes aplastic anemia and is now rare.

## Nucleic acid and metabolic inhibitors

**Fluoroquinolones** (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV; bactericidal and broad, but carry tendon rupture, QT prolongation, and CNS effects. **Rifampin** blocks RNA polymerase, turns secretions orange, and is never used alone because resistance develops quickly. **Metronidazole** is activated inside anaerobes and damages their DNA — the drug for anaerobes below the diaphragm, *C. difficile*, *Trichomonas* and *Giardia*.

**Sulfonamides and trimethoprim** block sequential steps in folate synthesis. Bacteria must make their own folate; we absorb ours from the diet — that is the selective toxicity. Given together as TMP-SMX, the blockade is synergistic and bactericidal.

**Isoniazid, ethambutol and pyrazinamide** target the mycobacterial cell wall; TB regimens use `RIPE` (rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) for `2 months` then rifampin plus isoniazid for `4 more`, because monotherapy breeds resistance in a slow-growing organism.

**Antifungals** target ergosterol: azoles inhibit its synthesis, amphotericin B binds it and forms pores, echinocandins block beta-glucan wall synthesis instead. **Antivirals** are mostly nucleoside analogs (acyclovir, which requires viral thymidine kinase for activation) or enzyme inhibitors (oseltamivir blocks neuraminidase; HIV therapy combines reverse transcriptase, integrase and protease inhibitors).

## Susceptibility testing

**Kirby-Bauer disk diffusion**: antibiotic disks on a lawn of organism, zone of inhibition measured in millimeters and compared to a standardized table to report S, I or R. Zone size alone does not rank potency across drugs.

**MIC** is the minimum inhibitory concentration — the lowest concentration preventing visible growth, by broth dilution or E-test gradient strip. **MBC** is the minimum bactericidal concentration, the lowest that kills `99.9%`.

> **On the exam:** Report a bigger zone as "susceptible," not as "stronger." And remember the therapeutic index: the higher the ratio of toxic dose to therapeutic dose, the safer the drug.
keyPoints: Selective toxicity targets what bacteria have and we do not: peptidoglycan, 70S ribosomes, folate synthesis, DNA gyrase.
Beta-lactams and vancomycin are bactericidal wall inhibitors; vancomycin is Gram-positive only.
30S inhibitors are aminoglycosides and tetracyclines; 50S inhibitors are macrolides, clindamycin and linezolid.
Broad-spectrum use causes superinfection: C. difficile colitis and Candida overgrowth.
MIC is the lowest concentration preventing growth; MBC kills 99.9%; Kirby-Bauer zones translate to S, I or R.

checks.q: A patient develops profuse diarrhea after 10 days of clindamycin. What happened?
choices: Superinfection with C. difficile after loss of normal flora
Malabsorption from the drug binding bile
checks.why: Broad anaerobic coverage eliminates competing colonic flora and lets C. difficile overgrow and release toxins. It is an ecological effect, not a direct toxicity or allergy.

checks.q: Why is vancomycin ineffective against E. coli?
choices: The molecule is too large to cross the Gram-negative outer membrane
checks.why: Gram-negatives have the D-Ala-D-Ala target, but the outer membrane physically excludes the large glycopeptide. Enzymatic hydrolysis of vancomycin is not a described mechanism and all bacteria have 70S ribosomes.

checks.q: Sulfonamides are selectively toxic because:
choices: Bacteria synthesize folate while humans absorb it from the diet
Sulfonamides only enter cells with 70S ribosomes
checks.why: The pathway, not the molecule, is the difference: bacteria must build folate from PABA and we take ours in preformed, so blocking synthesis spares us. Humans absolutely require folate, just not by synthesis.

lessons.title: Host-microbe interactions, virulence and epidemiology
lessons.body:
Most microbes on you are not trying to hurt you. The average adult carries roughly `10^13` human cells and at least as many bacterial cells. Disease is the exception, and it requires a specific set of conditions.

## Normal flora and relationships

**Resident microbiota** live on you permanently; **transient microbiota** pass through. They protect you by **microbial antagonism** — occupying attachment sites, consuming nutrients, and producing acids and bacteriocins. Wipe them out with antibiotics and the niche gets filled by something worse.

Relationships: **commensalism** (one benefits, the other unaffected), **mutualism** (both benefit — *E. coli* makes vitamin K for us), **parasitism** (one benefits, the host is harmed). An **opportunistic pathogen** is harmless in its usual place and dangerous when it moves or when the host weakens: *E. coli* is normal in the colon and causes urinary tract infection in the bladder.

> **Trap:** Skin, mouth, upper airway, GI tract and distal urethra all have normal flora. Blood, CSF, lower airway, bladder urine and deep tissues are normally **sterile** — an organism recovered there is almost always significant.

## Koch's postulates

1. The organism must be present in every case of the disease and absent in healthy hosts.
2. It must be isolated and grown in pure culture.
3. Inoculating a healthy susceptible host must reproduce the disease.
4. The organism must be re-isolated from that host and match.

The exceptions matter: organisms that cannot be cultured (*Treponema pallidum*, *Mycobacterium leprae*), diseases with no animal model, polymicrobial diseases, asymptomatic carriers, and one organism causing several diseases.

## Virulence factors

**Pathogenicity** is the ability to cause disease; **virulence** is the degree. **ID50** is the infectious dose for `50%` of hosts, and **LD50** is the lethal dose. Low ID50 means highly infectious — *Shigella* needs as few as `10–100` organisms, while *Vibrio cholerae* needs about `10^8`.

Entry is through **portals of entry**: mucous membranes (respiratory is most common), skin (hair follicles and breaks), or the **parenteral route** (punctures, bites, surgery). The right organism in the wrong portal often causes nothing.

Adherence uses adhesins on fimbriae, glycocalyx and spikes. Evasion uses capsules, M protein (*S. pyogenes*), coagulase (clots plasma to wall off the organism), leukocidins, IgA protease, and antigenic variation. Spread uses hyaluronidase and collagenase to digest connective tissue, and kinases to dissolve clots.

**Exotoxins** are secreted proteins from both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria. They are highly potent, specific, heat-labile, and convertible to **toxoids** for vaccines (tetanus, diphtheria). Types: A-B toxins (diphtheria, botulinum, cholera, tetanus), membrane-disrupting toxins (alpha-toxin, streptolysin), and **superantigens**, which nonspecifically activate huge numbers of T cells and dump cytokines — toxic shock syndrome.

**Endotoxin** is lipid A, Gram-negative only, part of the wall, released on lysis, heat-stable, weakly immunogenic, and always produces the same picture: fever, chills, hypotension, shock, DIC. There is no endotoxoid vaccine.

## Course of infection

Five stages: **incubation** (exposure to first symptom), **prodromal** (vague early symptoms), **illness** (peak, most severe), **decline**, **convalescence**. Communicability often peaks during the prodrome, before anyone knows they are sick.

Disease patterns: **acute** versus **chronic**; **latent** (dormant, reactivates); **local**, **focal**, **systemic**; **bacteremia** (bacteria in blood) versus **septicemia** (multiplying and causing illness); **primary** versus **secondary** infection; **subclinical** (no symptoms, still transmitting).

## Epidemiology

**Incidence** is new cases in a period; **prevalence** is total existing cases. **Sporadic** is occasional, **endemic** is constantly present in a region, **epidemic** is more than expected, **pandemic** is worldwide.

The **chain of infection**: infectious agent, reservoir, portal of exit, mode of transmission, portal of entry, susceptible host. Break any link and transmission stops — hand hygiene breaks contact transmission, masks break droplet and airborne, and immunization removes the susceptible host.

**Reservoirs** are human (including carriers), animal (**zoonoses** — rabies, Lyme, plague, brucellosis), or nonliving (soil for tetanus and botulism, water). **Transmission** is contact (direct, indirect via fomites, droplet at short range), vehicle (airborne on droplet nuclei of `5 micrometers` or less, which stay suspended and travel well beyond the short range of larger droplets, plus waterborne and foodborne), or **vector** (mechanical carriage on the body, or biological where the pathogen develops inside the arthropod).

**Healthcare-associated infection (HAI)**, formerly nosocomial, affects roughly `1 in 31` hospitalized patients on any given day in the United States. The big four are catheter-associated UTI (CAUTI), central-line-associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI), ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) and surgical site infection. Most are device-related, which is why the most effective intervention is removing the device as soon as it is not needed. **Herd immunity** protects the unvaccinated when enough of the population is immune — the threshold is about `95%` for measles and `80–85%` for polio.
keyPoints: Blood, CSF, lower airway, bladder urine and deep tissue are normally sterile; other surfaces carry protective normal flora.
Exotoxins are secreted, potent, heat-labile proteins convertible to toxoids; endotoxin is heat-stable lipid A causing fever and shock.
Koch's postulates fail for unculturable organisms, absent animal models, carriers and polymicrobial disease.
Chain of infection: agent, reservoir, portal of exit, transmission, portal of entry, susceptible host — break any link.
HAIs affect about 1 in 31 inpatients daily; CAUTI, CLABSI, VAP and SSI are mostly device-driven.

checks.q: A tampon-using patient presents with high fever, diffuse rash and hypotension. Blood cultures are negative. Which virulence mechanism best explains this?
choices: Superantigen exotoxin causing massive cytokine release
checks.why: TSST-1 is a superantigen: it cross-links T-cell receptors nonspecifically, so disease occurs without bloodstream invasion, explaining negative cultures. Endotoxin requires Gram-negative bacteremia and A-B neurotoxins cause paralysis, not rash.

checks.q: Which pairing of epidemiology terms is correct?
choices: Incidence is total existing cases; prevalence is new cases
Endemic means more cases than expected; epidemic means constantly present
Incidence is new cases; prevalence is total existing cases
Sporadic means worldwide; pandemic means occasional
checks.why: Incidence counts new cases in a defined period and prevalence counts all cases present. The other options invert endemic and epidemic or sporadic and pandemic.

checks.q: The single most effective intervention against catheter-associated urinary tract infection is:
choices: Removing the catheter as soon as it is no longer indicated
checks.why: Risk accrues per catheter-day, so eliminating device days removes the portal of entry. Prophylactic antibiotics select resistance and routine irrigation breaks the closed system, increasing risk.

lessons.title: Immunity, vaccines and the pathogens by body system
lessons.body:
## Innate immunity

Innate defenses are present at birth, act within minutes to hours, and are not specific to any one organism. First line: intact skin, mucous membranes, the mucociliary escalator, lysozyme in tears and saliva, stomach acid at pH `1.2–3.0`, normal flora, and flushing by urine and tears.

Second line: **phagocytes** (neutrophils first, then macrophages); **inflammation** with its four signs — redness, heat, swelling, pain; **fever**, when pyrogens including lipid A reset the hypothalamus; **complement**, a cascade of about 30 proteins activated by classical, alternative or lectin pathways, giving opsonization, chemotaxis, and the C5b-C9 **membrane attack complex** that lyses Gram-negative cells; and **interferons**, which warn neighboring cells to block viral replication. Toll-like receptors recognize conserved patterns (PAMPs) such as LPS and viral RNA.

## Adaptive immunity

Specific, slower on first exposure, and it remembers. An **antigen** is what the immune system recognizes; the piece actually bound is the **epitope**.

**Humoral immunity** comes from B cells, which mature in bone marrow; their plasma-cell descendants make antibodies against extracellular pathogens and toxins. **Cell-mediated immunity** comes from T cells, which mature in the thymus. Helper T cells (CD4) coordinate everything; cytotoxic T cells (CD8) kill virus-infected and tumor cells. HIV destroys CD4 cells, which is why it collapses both arms.

Antibody classes: **IgG** is `80%` of serum antibody, the only class crossing the placenta, and the main secondary-response antibody. **IgM** is the large pentamer, first produced in a new infection, best at complement fixation. **IgA** is the dimer in secretions and breast milk. **IgE** binds mast cells and drives allergy and parasite defense. **IgD** sits on B cells as a receptor.

The **primary response** takes `5–10 days` with mostly IgM and a low titer. The **secondary (anamnestic) response** is faster, larger and IgG-dominant because memory cells exist. That is the entire logic of boosters.

Four kinds of acquired immunity: naturally active (infection), naturally passive (maternal IgG across placenta, IgA in milk), artificially active (vaccination), artificially passive (immune globulin, antivenom — immediate but temporary, `weeks to months`).

**Vaccine types**: live attenuated (MMR, varicella, oral polio) give strong lifelong immunity but are contraindicated in pregnancy and in immunosuppression; inactivated (hepatitis A, injectable polio, most influenza) are safer but need boosters; subunit and conjugate (hepatitis B, HPV, Hib, pneumococcal) use purified pieces, with conjugation to protein making polysaccharides immunogenic in infants under `2 years`; toxoid (tetanus, diphtheria, boosted every `10 years`); mRNA (COVID-19).

**Serology** uses antibody-antigen specificity as a test: agglutination, ELISA, Western blot, immunofluorescence, rapid lateral-flow. A rising titer between acute and convalescent sera, or IgM, means recent infection; IgG alone means past exposure or vaccination.

> **Key:** IgM means now. IgG means before, or a booster response.

## Pathogens by body system

**Skin and wounds.** *Staphylococcus aureus* (folliculitis, abscess, impetigo, scalded skin syndrome; MRSA). *Streptococcus pyogenes* (impetigo, erysipelas, cellulitis, necrotizing fasciitis). *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* (burn wounds, hot-tub folliculitis, blue-green pigment and a grape-like odor). *Clostridium perfringens* (gas gangrene). Dermatophytes (tinea). Varicella-zoster (chickenpox, then shingles).

**Respiratory.** Upper: *Streptococcus pyogenes* pharyngitis (treat to prevent rheumatic fever), rhinoviruses. Lower: *Streptococcus pneumoniae* is the leading cause of community-acquired pneumonia, a Gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococcus. *Mycoplasma pneumoniae* causes walking pneumonia in the young. *Haemophilus influenzae* type b (epiglottitis, now rare because of the Hib conjugate vaccine). *Legionella pneumophila* from water systems and cooling towers. *Bordetella pertussis* (whooping cough). *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*: acid-fast, aerobic, forms granulomas, latent TB is positive on PPD or IGRA without disease. Influenza, RSV in infants, SARS-CoV-2.

**Gastrointestinal.** Infection (organism multiplies, longer incubation) versus intoxication (preformed toxin, onset in `1–6 hours`). *Staphylococcus aureus* and *Bacillus cereus* cause intoxication — vomiting fast, from reheated rice or picnic food. *Salmonella* (poultry and eggs), *Campylobacter jejuni* (the most common bacterial diarrhea in the US, associated with Guillain-Barre), *Shigella* (very low ID50, bloody), *E. coli* O157:H7 (Shiga toxin, hemolytic uremic syndrome — do **not** give antibiotics), *Vibrio cholerae* (rice-water stool), *C. difficile*, *Helicobacter pylori* (ulcers), norovirus, rotavirus, hepatitis A.

**Urogenital.** *E. coli* causes `80–90%` of uncomplicated UTIs. *Staphylococcus saprophyticus* in young women. *Neisseria gonorrhoeae* (Gram-negative diplococci in neutrophils). *Chlamydia trachomatis* is the most reported bacterial STI in the US and is often silent. *Treponema pallidum* (syphilis, three stages plus latency). HSV-2, HPV, *Trichomonas*, *Candida albicans*.

**Nervous system.** *Neisseria meningitidis* (petechial rash, dormitory outbreaks), *Streptococcus pneumoniae* (most common adult bacterial meningitis), *Listeria monocytogenes* (neonates, elderly, pregnancy), group B *Streptococcus* in newborns. *Clostridium tetani* (spastic paralysis, blocks inhibitory neurotransmitters) versus *Clostridium botulinum* (flaccid paralysis, blocks acetylcholine release). Rabies, poliovirus, *Cryptococcus neoformans* in AIDS, prions.

**Bloodborne and systemic.** HIV, hepatitis B and C, *Plasmodium* (malaria), *Borrelia burgdorferi* (Lyme disease, *Ixodes* tick, erythema migrans), *Rickettsia rickettsii* (Rocky Mountain spotted fever, rash moving from wrists and ankles inward), *Yersinia pestis*, *Epstein-Barr virus* (mononucleosis).

> **On the exam:** Tetanus is rigid, botulism is floppy. Both are *Clostridium*, both are A-B neurotoxins, and mixing them up is the most common single error in this unit.
keyPoints: Innate immunity is immediate and nonspecific; adaptive immunity is specific and remembers, with a faster IgG secondary response.
IgG is 80% of serum antibody and crosses the placenta; IgM appears first and signals current infection.
Live attenuated vaccines are contraindicated in pregnancy and immunosuppression; toxoid boosters every 10 years.
S. pneumoniae leads community-acquired pneumonia and adult bacterial meningitis; E. coli causes 80–90% of uncomplicated UTIs.
Tetanus causes spastic paralysis, botulism causes flaccid paralysis; E. coli O157:H7 should not be treated with antibiotics.

checks.q: A patient's serology shows IgM positive and IgG negative for hepatitis A. This indicates:
choices: A false positive because IgG is absent
checks.why: IgM is the first antibody produced and marks acute infection before class switching to IgG. IgG alone would indicate past infection or vaccination.

checks.q: Why must a live attenuated MMR vaccine be avoided during pregnancy?
choices: The attenuated virus can replicate and pose fetal risk
It requires an adjuvant that crosses the placenta
checks.why: Live vaccines replicate in the host, which is why they are strong but also why they are contraindicated in pregnancy and immunosuppression. Inactivated and toxoid vaccines carry no such risk.

checks.q: A child with bloody diarrhea after eating undercooked ground beef develops kidney failure. Which statement is correct?
choices: Antibiotics should be given immediately to shorten illness
Antibiotics may increase Shiga toxin release and worsen hemolytic uremic syndrome
The illness is an intoxication with 1–6 hour onset
checks.why: E. coli O157:H7 lysis releases more Shiga toxin, so antibiotics are associated with higher HUS risk and care is supportive. The history and HUS point away from Campylobacter, and the incubation is days, not hours.

cards.front: What is the practical resolution limit of a light microscope?
cards.back: About 0.2 micrometers. Bacteria (0.2–2 micrometers wide) are visible; viruses (20–300 nanometers) are not and need electron microscopy.

cards.front: Why is immersion oil used with the 100x objective?
cards.back: Oil has the same refractive index as glass, so light rays are not bent away and lost. It improves resolution, not magnification.

cards.front: List the four Gram stain steps in order and the result of each.
cards.back: Crystal violet (all purple), Gram's iodine mordant (traps complex), alcohol decolorizer (critical step), safranin counterstain (Gram-negatives turn pink).

cards.front: What does an acid-fast stain detect, and in which organisms?
cards.back: Mycolic acid in the wall of Mycobacterium and Nocardia. Carbolfuchsin driven in with heat resists acid-alcohol decolorization; everything else takes methylene blue.

cards.front: What did Pasteur's swan-neck flask experiment prove?
cards.back: It disproved spontaneous generation. Broth stayed sterile while the neck trapped airborne microbes, but grew when tipped so broth reached the bend.

cards.front: Why are most bacterial stains basic (cationic) dyes?
cards.back: Bacterial surfaces carry a net negative charge, so positively charged basic dyes such as crystal violet, methylene blue and safranin are attracted to them.

cards.front: How does a capsule stain work and why?
cards.back: It is a negative stain (India ink). Capsules do not take up dye, so the capsule appears as a clear halo around a stained cell against a dark background.

cards.front: What two sugars make up peptidoglycan and what cross-links them?
cards.back: N-acetylglucosamine (NAG) and N-acetylmuramic acid (NAM), alternating, cross-linked by short peptide bridges. Penicillin blocks the cross-linking.

cards.front: Structurally, how do Gram-positive and Gram-negative walls differ?
cards.back: Gram-positive: thick peptidoglycan (20–80 nanometers) with teichoic acids. Gram-negative: thin peptidoglycan (2–7 nanometers) plus an outer membrane with LPS and porins.

cards.front: What are the three parts of LPS and which one is endotoxin?
cards.back: O antigen (serotyping), core polysaccharide, and lipid A. Lipid A is endotoxin: fever, vasodilation, hypotension, shock, DIC on cell lysis.

cards.front: Difference between fimbriae and a sex pilus?
cards.back: Fimbriae are short, numerous, and used for adhesion to surfaces. A sex pilus is longer, one or two per cell, and transfers DNA during conjugation.

cards.front: Why is the 70S bacterial ribosome clinically important?
cards.back: Human ribosomes are 80S. That difference gives selective toxicity to aminoglycosides and tetracyclines (30S) and macrolides, clindamycin and linezolid (50S).

cards.front: Which two genera form endospores, and what conditions do spores survive?
cards.back: Bacillus and Clostridium, both Gram-positive rods. Spores survive boiling, drying, radiation and most disinfectants; an autoclave is required to kill them.

cards.front: What does a bacterial capsule do for the organism?
cards.back: It blocks phagocytosis and hides surface antigens. S. pneumoniae, K. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis and H. influenzae rely on it; capsular vaccines target it.

cards.front: Which bacterium has no cell wall and what does that mean for treatment?
cards.back: Mycoplasma. With no peptidoglycan, beta-lactams are useless; M. pneumoniae is treated with macrolides, tetracyclines or fluoroquinolones.

cards.front: What is a plasmid and why does it matter?
cards.back: A small circular extrachromosomal DNA molecule, not required for survival, that often carries antibiotic resistance genes (R factors), toxin genes or conjugation machinery.

cards.front: What are fungal cell walls and membranes made of?
cards.back: Walls are chitin (not peptidoglycan). Membranes use ergosterol instead of cholesterol — the target of azoles and amphotericin B.

cards.front: Define a dimorphic fungus and name four.
cards.back: Mold at 25 degrees Celsius in the environment, yeast at 37 degrees Celsius in the body. Histoplasma, Blastomyces, Coccidioides, Sporothrix.

cards.front: Which protozoa resist chlorination and how are they removed from water?
cards.back: Giardia lamblia and Cryptosporidium cysts/oocysts. Filtration removes them; standard chlorination does not reliably kill them.

cards.front: Name the apicomplexans and their diseases.
cards.back: Plasmodium (malaria, female Anopheles mosquito), Toxoplasma gondii (cat feces, undercooked meat; pregnancy and AIDS risk), Cryptosporidium (watery diarrhea).

cards.front: What lab finding suggests a helminth infection?
cards.back: Peripheral eosinophilia on a CBC. Diagnosis is confirmed by ova and parasites in stool, or the cellophane tape test for pinworm.

cards.front: Which fungi are opportunistic and who gets sick from them?
cards.back: Candida, Aspergillus, Pneumocystis jirovecii and Cryptococcus neoformans — disease in the immunocompromised: HIV, chemotherapy, transplant, prolonged steroids.

cards.front: Difference between a yeast and a mold?
cards.back: Yeasts are single cells reproducing by budding. Molds grow as filamentous hyphae forming a mycelium; hyphae may be septate or coenocytic.

cards.front: What are the five steps of animal virus replication?
cards.back: Attachment to a receptor, penetration and uncoating, biosynthesis, assembly (maturation), release by lysis (naked) or budding (enveloped).

cards.front: Why do naked viruses spread through surfaces and food?
cards.back: They have only a protein capsid with no lipid envelope, so alcohol, detergents and drying do not destroy them. Norovirus and hepatitis A are the examples.

cards.front: What is lysogenic conversion and which toxins come from it?
cards.back: A prophage integrated in the bacterial chromosome gives the cell new traits. Diphtheria, botulinum, cholera, erythrogenic and Shiga toxins are phage-encoded.

cards.front: What do reverse transcriptase and integrase do in a retrovirus?
cards.back: Reverse transcriptase makes DNA from the +ssRNA genome; integrase inserts that DNA into the host chromosome as a permanent provirus.

cards.front: Name four oncogenic viruses and the cancers they cause.
cards.back: HPV 16 and 18 (cervical), hepatitis B and C (hepatocellular carcinoma), Epstein-Barr (Burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma), HHV-8 (Kaposi sarcoma).

cards.front: What is a prion and why is it so hard to destroy?
cards.back: An infectious misfolded protein (PrP-Sc) with no nucleic acid that converts normal PrP-C. It resists autoclaving, formalin and radiation; decontamination needs 1 N NaOH plus extended autoclaving.

cards.front: What is cytopathic effect and why is it used?
cards.back: Visible damage to cultured cells from viral infection — inclusion bodies, syncytia, rounding. It is how a lab confirms a virus grew in cell culture.

cards.front: How do you calculate cells after n generations?
cards.back: N = N0 times 2^n. Example: 100 cells, E. coli at a 20-minute generation time for 3 hours, is 9 generations = 100 x 512 = 51,200 cells.

cards.front: Name the four phases of the bacterial growth curve and what happens in each.
cards.back: Lag (adapting, no division), log (constant doubling, most antibiotic-susceptible), stationary (births equal deaths, spores and toxins), death (exponential decline).

cards.front: Give the generation time of E. coli and of M. tuberculosis.
cards.back: E. coli about 20 minutes; M. tuberculosis 15–20 hours. That is why TB cultures take 6–8 weeks and treatment runs 6–9 months.

cards.front: List the five oxygen requirement classes with an example of each.
cards.back: Obligate aerobe (M. tuberculosis), obligate anaerobe (Clostridium), facultative anaerobe (E. coli), aerotolerant anaerobe (Lactobacillus), microaerophile (Campylobacter).

cards.front: Which enzymes protect cells from toxic oxygen products?
cards.back: Superoxide dismutase and catalase. Obligate anaerobes lack them. The catalase test separates Staphylococcus (positive) from Streptococcus (negative).

cards.front: Compare ATP yield: aerobic respiration versus fermentation.
cards.back: Aerobic respiration nets about 38 ATP per glucose in prokaryotes. Fermentation nets only 2 ATP but regenerates NAD+ and makes identifiable acids and gases.

cards.front: What makes MacConkey agar both selective and differential?
cards.back: Bile salts and crystal violet inhibit Gram-positives (selective); lactose plus a pH indicator turns lactose fermenters pink (differential).

cards.front: How do you compute CFU/mL from a plate count?
cards.back: CFU/mL = colonies divided by (dilution factor x volume plated). Use plates with 25–250 colonies. Example: 60 colonies, 10^-4 dilution, 0.1 mL = 6.0 x 10^6 CFU/mL.

cards.front: Which pathogen grows at refrigerator temperature, and why does it matter?
cards.back: Listeria monocytogenes. It multiplies at 4 degrees Celsius, so deli meats, soft cheeses and refrigerated ready-to-eat foods transmit it, especially in pregnancy.

cards.front: Define sterilization, disinfection and antisepsis.
cards.back: Sterilization destroys all microbial life including spores. Disinfection kills pathogens on inanimate objects. Antisepsis is the same process applied to living tissue.

cards.front: What are the standard autoclave parameters and how is the cycle verified?
cards.back: 121 degrees Celsius at 15 psi for 15 minutes with steam contacting all surfaces. Verified with a biological indicator of Geobacillus stearothermophilus spores.

cards.front: Why is 70% alcohol more effective than 95–100% alcohol?
cards.back: Water is required for protein denaturation. Absolute alcohol dehydrates and coagulates the surface without penetrating. No concentration of alcohol kills spores.

cards.front: Rank microbial resistance to control agents from easiest to hardest to kill.
cards.back: Enveloped viruses, Gram-positive bacteria, Gram-negative bacteria, fungi, naked viruses, mycobacteria, endospores, prions.

cards.front: Give the three pasteurization schedules.
cards.back: Batch 63 degrees Celsius for 30 minutes; high-temperature short-time 72 degrees Celsius for 15 seconds; ultra-high temperature 140 degrees Celsius for 3 seconds (sterile).

cards.front: How does UV radiation kill, and what is its main limitation?
cards.back: UV at 260 nanometers forms thymine dimers that block DNA replication. It does not penetrate glass, plastic, dirt or tissue, so it is surface and air only.

cards.front: Which pathogens require soap-and-water handwashing rather than alcohol foam?
cards.back: Clostridioides difficile (endospores) and norovirus (naked virus). Alcohol does not kill them; friction and rinsing physically remove them, and rooms get bleach.

cards.front: What filter pore size sterilizes a heat-sensitive liquid?
cards.back: A 0.22 micrometer membrane filter retains bacteria. It is used for vaccines, antibiotics and heat-labile media; HEPA filters do the equivalent job for air.

cards.front: Name the four types of point and frameshift mutations.
cards.back: Silent (same amino acid), missense (different amino acid), nonsense (premature stop), and frameshift from insertion or deletion not in multiples of three.

cards.front: Compare transformation, transduction and conjugation.
cards.back: Transformation: uptake of naked DNA by a competent cell. Transduction: bacteriophage carries bacterial DNA. Conjugation: direct transfer of a plasmid through a sex pilus.

cards.front: Why do R plasmids cause multidrug resistance so quickly?
cards.back: One plasmid can carry several resistance genes and moves by conjugation even between species, so a single transfer event converts a susceptible organism to multidrug-resistant.

cards.front: What are the five general mechanisms of antibiotic resistance?
cards.back: Enzymatic destruction (beta-lactamase), target alteration (mecA/PBP2a), decreased permeability (porin loss), efflux pumps, and bypass or overproduction of the target.

cards.front: What genetic changes make MRSA and VRE resistant?
cards.back: MRSA: mecA encodes PBP2a, a penicillin-binding protein beta-lactams cannot bind. VRE: the peptidoglycan terminus changes from D-Ala-D-Ala to D-Ala-D-Lac.

cards.front: What does the Ames test measure?
cards.back: Mutagenicity. A histidine-requiring Salmonella strain reverting to growth without histidine indicates the chemical causes mutations, which correlates with carcinogenicity.

cards.front: Do antibiotics create resistant bacteria?
cards.back: No. They select for rare pre-existing mutants by killing the susceptible majority. Mutations at roughly 1 in 10^9 per base already exist in any large population.

cards.front: What is selective toxicity and what are the classic bacterial targets?
cards.back: Harming the microbe more than the host by attacking structures we lack: peptidoglycan, the 70S ribosome, folate synthesis from PABA, and DNA gyrase.

cards.front: How do beta-lactams work, and what does a beta-lactamase inhibitor add?
cards.back: Beta-lactams bind penicillin-binding proteins and block peptidoglycan cross-linking. Clavulanate or tazobactam has little activity itself; it protects the partner drug from hydrolysis.

cards.front: Which antibiotics hit the 30S subunit and which hit the 50S?
cards.back: 30S: aminoglycosides (cidal) and tetracyclines (static). 50S: macrolides, clindamycin, linezolid, chloramphenicol.

cards.front: Why is vancomycin useless against Gram-negative bacteria?
cards.back: The glycopeptide is too large to cross the Gram-negative outer membrane, even though the D-Ala-D-Ala target is present. It is Gram-positive coverage only.

cards.front: Define MIC and MBC.
cards.back: MIC is the lowest drug concentration preventing visible growth. MBC is the lowest concentration killing 99.9% of the inoculum. Kirby-Bauer zones report S, I or R instead.

cards.front: What is superinfection and which drugs cause it most?
cards.back: Overgrowth of a resistant organism after broad-spectrum therapy wipes out normal flora. Clindamycin, fluoroquinolones and cephalosporins are classic causes of C. difficile colitis.

cards.front: What is the standard TB regimen and why is it four drugs?
cards.back: RIPE — rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol — for 2 months, then rifampin plus isoniazid for 4 more. Monotherapy in a slow-growing organism rapidly selects resistance.

cards.front: Which drug covers anaerobes below the diaphragm, C. difficile, Trichomonas and Giardia?
cards.back: Metronidazole. It is reduced to a toxic radical only inside anaerobic organisms, which damages their DNA — the source of its selectivity.

cards.front: Which body sites are normally sterile?
cards.back: Blood, cerebrospinal fluid, lower respiratory tract, bladder urine and deep tissues. An organism recovered from these sites is almost always clinically significant.

cards.front: State Koch's postulates and two exceptions.
cards.back: Present in every case, isolated in pure culture, reproduces disease on inoculation, re-isolated. Fails for unculturable organisms (T. pallidum, M. leprae) and asymptomatic carriers.
