cards.front: Compare exotoxin and endotoxin.
cards.back: Exotoxin: secreted protein, Gram-positive or negative, potent, specific, heat-labile, makes a toxoid vaccine. Endotoxin: lipid A, Gram-negative wall, released on lysis, heat-stable, causes fever and shock.

cards.front: What is a superantigen and what does it cause?
cards.back: A toxin that nonspecifically cross-links T-cell receptors, activating huge numbers of T cells and releasing a flood of cytokines. TSST-1 causes toxic shock syndrome.

cards.front: Name the six links in the chain of infection.
cards.back: Infectious agent, reservoir, portal of exit, mode of transmission, portal of entry, susceptible host. Breaking any single link stops transmission.

cards.front: List the five stages in the course of an infectious disease.
cards.back: Incubation, prodromal, illness (peak), decline, convalescence. Communicability is often highest during the prodrome, before the diagnosis is made.

cards.front: What are the four major healthcare-associated infections?
cards.back: CAUTI, CLABSI, ventilator-associated pneumonia and surgical site infection. About 1 in 31 US inpatients has an HAI on a given day; most are device-related.

cards.front: Difference between incidence and prevalence?
cards.back: Incidence is the number of new cases in a defined period. Prevalence is all existing cases at a point in time, including old ones.

cards.front: What do the five antibody classes do?
cards.back: IgG 80% of serum, crosses placenta, secondary response. IgM pentamer, first and best at complement. IgA dimer in secretions. IgE mast cells, allergy and parasites. IgD B-cell receptor.

cards.front: Why is the secondary immune response faster and larger?
cards.back: Memory B and T cells already exist, so antibody appears in 1–3 days instead of 5–10, at higher titer, and is mostly IgG rather than IgM. That is why boosters work.

cards.front: Which vaccine types exist and who cannot receive live attenuated ones?
cards.back: Live attenuated, inactivated, subunit/conjugate, toxoid, mRNA. Live vaccines are contraindicated in pregnancy and immunosuppression because the organism still replicates.

cards.front: What does complement do once activated?
cards.back: Opsonization, chemotaxis of phagocytes, inflammation, and formation of the C5b-C9 membrane attack complex that lyses Gram-negative cells. Activated by classical, alternative or lectin pathways.

cards.front: Tetanus versus botulism: which is rigid and which is floppy?
cards.back: Clostridium tetani blocks inhibitory neurotransmitters, causing spastic (rigid) paralysis. Clostridium botulinum blocks acetylcholine release, causing flaccid (floppy) paralysis.

quiz.q: A technologist Gram stains a 48-hour Staphylococcus aureus culture and reports pink cocci in clusters. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: Aging cells lose wall integrity and over-decolorize
The isolate is actually a Gram-negative coccus
quiz.why: Old cultures have damaged peptidoglycan and release the crystal violet-iodine complex during decolorization. Under-decolorizing would make cells falsely purple, and omitting crystal violet would leave them pink but the arrangement would still be described.

quiz.q: Which statement about magnification and resolution is correct?
choices: Electron microscopes have lower resolution but higher magnification
Immersion oil increases total magnification to 1000x
Resolution is the ability to distinguish two close points as separate
quiz.why: Resolution is about clarity and separation of adjacent points; magnification only enlarges. Oil improves resolution by preventing refraction loss, and electron microscopes exceed light microscopes in both measures.

quiz.q: A sputum specimen stains red against a blue background after carbolfuchsin, heat and acid-alcohol. Which organism is most consistent?
quiz.why: Retaining carbolfuchsin through acid-alcohol defines acid-fastness, caused by mycolic acid in Mycobacterium. S. pneumoniae and Klebsiella are seen on Gram stain, and Mycoplasma has no wall and stains poorly with anything.

quiz.q: Which structure is responsible for the septic shock seen when a Gram-negative bloodstream infection is treated?
quiz.why: Lipid A is the endotoxic portion of LPS and is released when the outer membrane breaks apart. O antigen is used for serotyping, teichoic acid is Gram-positive, and peptidoglycan is not the shock trigger.

quiz.q: A soil-contaminated wound is irrigated and the patient is told boiling water would not have sterilized the instrument used. Which structure justifies that statement?
quiz.why: Endospores from Clostridium and Bacillus survive boiling at 100 degrees Celsius; only an autoclave, dry heat at 170 degrees Celsius for 2 hours, or a chemical sterilant destroys them. Capsules and slime layers offer no heat protection.

quiz.q: Which pairing of bacterial structure and function is correct?
choices: Sex pilus mediates adhesion to epithelium
Teichoic acid forms the outer membrane
quiz.why: Capsules prevent engulfment by phagocytes. Fimbriae adhere and sex pili transfer DNA — the reverse of the first two options — and teichoic acid is embedded in Gram-positive peptidoglycan, not in an outer membrane.

quiz.q: A soil fungus grows as filamentous mold on Sabouraud agar at room temperature but as budding yeast in tissue at body temperature. Which organism fits?
quiz.why: Histoplasma is dimorphic, mold at 25 degrees Celsius and yeast at 37 degrees Celsius. Candida is a yeast, Aspergillus is always a mold, and Trichophyton is a dermatophyte mold.

quiz.q: A hiker who drank untreated stream water develops two weeks of greasy, foul-smelling diarrhea and bloating without blood or fever. Which organism is most likely?
quiz.why: Giardia produces malabsorptive, fatty, non-bloody diarrhea from untreated surface water. Entamoeba and Shigella cause bloody dysentery, and cholera produces massive watery rice-water stool over days, not weeks.

quiz.q: Amphotericin B works by:
choices: Binding ergosterol and forming membrane pores
quiz.why: Amphotericin B binds existing ergosterol and creates pores, so it is fungicidal. Azoles inhibit ergosterol synthesis, echinocandins block beta-glucan wall synthesis, and no clinical antifungal targets 80S ribosomes.

quiz.q: Which is true of all viruses?
choices: They contain both DNA and RNA
They contain either DNA or RNA, never both
quiz.why: A virus carries a single nucleic acid type. Envelopes are present in only some viruses, and binary fission is a cellular process viruses cannot perform since they lack ribosomes and metabolism.

quiz.q: A patient with a history of chickenpox at age 6 develops a painful unilateral dermatomal rash at age 68. This is best explained by:
choices: An autoimmune reaction to prior vaccination
Reactivation of latent virus in a dorsal root ganglion
quiz.why: Varicella-zoster persists latently in sensory ganglia and reactivates as shingles when cell-mediated immunity wanes, producing a dermatomal pattern. Reinfection would not follow a single dermatome, and lysogenic conversion applies to bacteriophages.

quiz.q: Why are prions the most difficult infectious agents to destroy?
choices: They have a double lipid envelope
They are proteins with no nucleic acid to damage
They replicate faster than any bacterium
quiz.why: Standard sterilization targets nucleic acid and denatures ordinary proteins, but the PrP-Sc conformation resists both, so extended autoclaving with 1 N NaOH is required. Prions have no envelope, no spores, and no replication machinery of their own.

quiz.q: HIV specifically destroys helper T cells because:
choices: gp120 binds the CD4 receptor plus a chemokine co-receptor
Reverse transcriptase only works in lymphocytes
The virus is a naked icosahedral particle
quiz.why: Tropism is determined by receptor fit, and gp120 binds CD4 with CCR5 or CXCR4. Reverse transcriptase functions in any infected cell, and HIV is enveloped, not naked.

quiz.q: A culture of 200 cells with a 20-minute generation time grows for 2 hours. Final count?
quiz.why: Two hours at 20 minutes per doubling is 6 generations: 200 x 2^6 = 200 x 64 = 12,800. Multiplying 200 by 6 gives the wrong 1,200, and using 5 or 7 generations gives 6,400 or 25,600.

quiz.q: An organism grows only in the narrow band just below the surface of a thioglycolate tube. It is best classified as:
quiz.why: A band below the surface indicates a requirement for reduced oxygen, roughly 2–10%. Obligate aerobes grow at the very top, obligate anaerobes only at the bottom, and aerotolerant organisms grow evenly throughout.

quiz.q: Which phase of the growth curve is associated with endospore formation and exotoxin production?
quiz.why: Nutrient depletion and waste accumulation in stationary phase trigger sporulation and secondary metabolite production. Log phase cells are dividing maximally, and death phase cells are dying exponentially.

quiz.q: A urine culture plated at a 1:1000 dilution with 0.1 mL yields 150 colonies. The original count is:
quiz.why: 150 divided by (10^-3 x 0.1) = 150 / 10^-4 = 1.5 x 10^6 CFU/mL. Ignoring the 0.1 mL plated volume yields the incorrect 1.5 x 10^5.

quiz.q: An instrument is autoclaved but the biological indicator still shows growth. Which is the most likely cause?
choices: The load was packed so steam could not contact all surfaces
Geobacillus spores are not killed by any autoclave cycle
Wet heat is less effective than dry heat
quiz.why: Steam must directly contact every surface; overpacking and trapped air are the usual failure modes. G. stearothermophilus spores are precisely the standard a working cycle must kill, and moist heat is more efficient than dry heat.

quiz.q: Which term describes reducing microbial numbers on a living surface such as skin before an injection?
quiz.why: Antisepsis applies to living tissue. Disinfection is for inanimate objects, sanitization lowers counts to a public-health standard on utensils and surfaces, and sterilization is absolute destruction of all life.

quiz.q: Which control method is bacteriostatic rather than bactericidal?
quiz.why: Cold slows metabolism without killing, and organisms resume growth on warming. Autoclaving, incineration and ethylene oxide are sterilizing methods that destroy organisms including spores.

quiz.q: A hospital changes from alcohol foam to soap and water for a specific isolation type. Which pathogen prompted the change?
quiz.why: C. difficile spores resist alcohol, so mechanical removal by handwashing plus bleach cleaning is required. Influenza and RSV are enveloped and MRSA is a vegetative bacterium, all of which alcohol handles well.

quiz.q: A previously susceptible Klebsiella isolate becomes resistant to three unrelated antibiotic classes within one hospitalization. Which mechanism best explains the speed?
choices: Acquisition of an R plasmid by conjugation
quiz.why: R plasmids carry multiple resistance genes and transfer in a single conjugation event, even between species. Sequential independent mutations are far too improbable over days, and lysogenic conversion typically supplies toxin genes.

quiz.q: Griffith's experiment in which heat-killed virulent pneumococci made live avirulent pneumococci lethal demonstrated:
quiz.why: The live R strain took up naked DNA released by the dead S strain, which is transformation. Transduction requires a phage vector and conjugation requires cell-to-cell contact through a pilus, neither of which was present.

quiz.q: A Staphylococcus aureus isolate is resistant to oxacillin, cefazolin and amoxicillin-clavulanate. Which mechanism is present?
quiz.why: Resistance to a beta-lactamase inhibitor combination and to cephalosporins indicates target alteration rather than enzyme production, which is mecA encoding PBP2a. Clavulanate would restore activity if a simple beta-lactamase were the mechanism.

quiz.q: Which type of mutation is most likely to abolish protein function entirely?
quiz.why: A frameshift shifts every downstream codon, scrambling the whole remaining sequence. Silent and synonymous changes do not alter the amino acid, and a missense change alters only one residue, which may be tolerated.

quiz.q: A patient with severe penicillin anaphylaxis needs coverage for a Gram-negative bacteremia. Which agent is safest with respect to cross-reactivity?
quiz.why: Aztreonam is a monobactam with negligible cross-reactivity with penicillins and covers aerobic Gram-negatives. Cephalosporins and carbapenems share the bicyclic beta-lactam structure, and amoxicillin is a penicillin.

quiz.q: Which antibiotic class carries a documented risk of nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity requiring drug level monitoring?
quiz.why: Gentamicin, tobramycin and amikacin damage the kidney and eighth cranial nerve, so peaks and troughs are followed. Macrolides prolong QT, tetracyclines stain teeth, and sulfonamides cause rash and hypersensitivity.

quiz.q: Kirby-Bauer testing shows a 22 mm zone for drug A and a 14 mm zone for drug B. What can you correctly conclude?
choices: Drug A is more potent than drug B
Zone diameters must be compared to drug-specific breakpoint tables
Drug B is inactive against the organism
Drug A has a lower MIC than drug B
quiz.why: Zone size depends on diffusion characteristics unique to each drug, so raw millimeters are only meaningful against that drug's standardized interpretive table. Comparing zones between different drugs says nothing about relative potency or MIC.

quiz.q: Which statement about bacteriostatic drugs is accurate?
choices: They are always preferred over bactericidal drugs
They are contraindicated in all infections
They rely on host immune function to clear the infection
quiz.why: Static drugs halt replication but the immune system must eliminate the organisms, which is why cidal agents are chosen for neutropenia, endocarditis and meningitis. They do not lyse walls and are perfectly appropriate in immunocompetent patients.

quiz.q: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is selectively toxic because bacteria:
choices: Must synthesize folate rather than absorb it
quiz.why: Human cells take up preformed dietary folate, while bacteria build it from PABA, so blocking two sequential synthesis steps spares us. Bacteria have 70S ribosomes and do possess DNA gyrase, which is a different drug target.

quiz.q: An organism cultured from cerebrospinal fluid is reported. Why is this automatically significant?
choices: CSF has abundant normal flora that is usually harmless
CSF cultures are frequently contaminated by skin flora
quiz.why: CSF, blood, lower airway, bladder urine and deep tissue have no normal flora, so any recovered organism demands explanation. Skin contamination can occur but is the exception, not the default assumption.

quiz.q: Four hours after a church picnic, several attendees develop sudden vomiting and cramping without fever. Which mechanism and organism fit best?
choices: Infection with Salmonella after 24 hours of replication
Intoxication by preformed Staphylococcus aureus enterotoxin
Shiga toxin production by E. coli O157:H7
quiz.why: Onset within 1–6 hours with vomiting and no fever indicates preformed toxin ingested with the food, not organism replication. Salmonella, Shigella and O157:H7 all require an incubation period measured in days and typically produce fever or bloody stool.

quiz.q: Koch's postulates cannot be fulfilled for syphilis primarily because Treponema pallidum:
choices: Has no known portal of entry
Cannot be grown in pure culture on artificial media
Is found in healthy hosts as normal flora
quiz.why: The second postulate requires pure culture, and T. pallidum cannot be cultivated on standard media. It has a clear sexual and transplacental portal of entry, real virulence factors, and is never normal flora.

quiz.q: Which intervention breaks the chain of infection at the 'susceptible host' link?
quiz.why: Vaccination removes susceptibility in the host. Hand hygiene and surface disinfection interrupt the mode of transmission, and isolation controls the portal of exit and transmission.

quiz.q: A newborn is protected from measles for several months without ever being vaccinated. This is an example of:
quiz.why: Maternal IgG crossing the placenta is passive and natural, and it wanes over months. Active immunity requires the infant's own response, and artificial passive immunity would mean injected immune globulin.

quiz.q: A college freshman in a dormitory develops fever, neck stiffness and a rapidly spreading petechial rash. Which organism is most likely?
quiz.why: The petechial or purpuric rash with meningitis in a dormitory setting is characteristic of meningococcus. S. pneumoniae causes meningitis without that rash, Listeria targets neonates and the elderly, and Cryptococcus causes indolent meningitis in AIDS.

quiz.q: Which antibody class appears first in a new infection and is the best complement activator?
quiz.why: IgM is a pentamer with ten binding sites, produced first and highly efficient at fixing complement. IgG dominates the secondary response, IgA protects secretions, and IgE mediates allergy.

quiz.q: A 4-year-old has been exposed to a household case of pertussis. Which statement about the acellular pertussis vaccine is accurate?
choices: It is a live attenuated vaccine contraindicated in children
It cannot be given with other vaccines
It provides lifelong immunity after one dose
It is a subunit vaccine and requires a series plus later boosters
quiz.why: Acellular pertussis uses purified antigens, so immunity is safer but wanes and requires a primary series plus Tdap boosters. It is not live, one dose is insufficient, and it is routinely co-administered in combination vaccines.

scenarios.title: Lab practical: identifying an unknown from a wound culture
scenarios.intro: You are at the bench in microbiology lab. Your instructor hands you a broth tube labeled **Unknown 14**, drawn from a simulated wound culture, and a worksheet. You have blood agar, MacConkey agar, mannitol salt agar, Gram stain reagents, hydrogen peroxide, and a coagulase kit. The rule is the same as in a clinical lab: cheap tests first, and every step should narrow the field.

steps.prompt: The broth is turbid after overnight incubation at `37 degrees Celsius`. Nothing else is known. What is your first move?

choices.text: Perform a Gram stain from the broth
choices.feedback: Correct. The Gram stain is the first test on virtually any clinical specimen because it splits the universe of possibilities in two minutes for pennies.

choices.text: Run a coagulase test immediately
choices.feedback: Premature. Coagulase only distinguishes S. aureus from other staphylococci. Running it before you know the organism is even a Gram-positive coccus wastes reagent and tells you nothing interpretable.

choices.text: Streak to MacConkey agar and wait 24 hours
choices.feedback: Not wrong, but slow and narrow. MacConkey only grows Gram-negatives, so if the organism is Gram-positive you have burned a full day learning nothing.

choices.text: Send the broth for acid-fast staining
choices.feedback: Harmful use of resources. Acid-fast staining is reserved for suspected Mycobacterium or Nocardia, and neither grows to turbidity overnight in routine broth.

steps.prompt: The Gram stain shows **purple cocci in grape-like clusters**. Name the two facts you now have and choose the next test.

choices.text: Gram-positive cocci in clusters; run a catalase test with hydrogen peroxide
choices.feedback: Exactly right. Clusters point to Staphylococcus or Micrococcus; catalase separates staphylococci (positive, bubbles) from streptococci (negative).

choices.text: Gram-negative cocci; streak to MacConkey
choices.feedback: Misread. Purple means the crystal violet-iodine complex was retained, which is Gram-positive. MacConkey would show no growth and cost you a day.

choices.text: Gram-positive cocci in chains; test for bile solubility
choices.feedback: Arrangement matters. Chains suggest Streptococcus; clusters suggest Staphylococcus. Bile solubility is a pneumococcal test and does not apply here.

choices.text: Gram-positive rods; check for endospores with malachite green
choices.feedback: Shape misread. Cocci are spheres, not rods, and staphylococci do not form endospores — only Bacillus and Clostridium do.

steps.prompt: Hydrogen peroxide produces vigorous bubbling. The isolate is **catalase positive**. You streak mannitol salt agar, which contains `7.5%` NaCl and mannitol with phenol red. What are you testing for, and what result would point to S. aureus?

choices.text: Salt tolerance and mannitol fermentation; S. aureus grows and turns the agar yellow
choices.feedback: Correct on both counts. The 7.5% salt is the selective element and the acid from mannitol fermentation drops the pH, turning phenol red yellow.

choices.text: Hemolysis pattern; S. aureus produces a clear zone
choices.feedback: Wrong medium. Hemolysis is read on blood agar. Mannitol salt has no red blood cells in it.

choices.text: Lactose fermentation; S. aureus turns colonies pink
choices.feedback: That is MacConkey logic applied to the wrong plate. Mannitol salt tests mannitol, and its indicator turns yellow, not pink.

choices.text: Oxygen requirement; S. aureus grows only at the bottom of the plate
choices.feedback: Plates do not measure oxygen gradients; thioglycolate tubes do. S. aureus is a facultative anaerobe and grows across the whole plate.

steps.prompt: The mannitol salt plate is bright yellow with growth, and the coagulase test clots the plasma. Your unknown is **Staphylococcus aureus**. Your instructor adds one line to the worksheet: the simulated patient's isolate is also resistant to oxacillin. What does that tell you about the mechanism and the treatment?

choices.text: mecA encodes PBP2a, so all beta-lactams fail; vancomycin or linezolid is appropriate
choices.feedback: Correct. Oxacillin resistance is the marker for MRSA, and because the target itself is altered, adding a beta-lactamase inhibitor does not help. Vancomycin, linezolid, daptomycin or ceftaroline are the options.

choices.text: The organism makes beta-lactamase, so amoxicillin-clavulanate will work
choices.feedback: This is the classic error. Oxacillin and nafcillin are already beta-lactamase resistant, so failing them proves the mechanism is target alteration, not enzyme production. Clavulanate adds nothing.

choices.text: Resistance was caused by exposure to oxacillin creating a new mutation
choices.feedback: Antibiotics select, they do not create. The mecA gene arrived by horizontal transfer on a mobile element; exposure simply removed the susceptible competition.

choices.text: Report the isolate as susceptible since it grew on mannitol salt agar
choices.feedback: Growth on a selective medium is an identification result, not a susceptibility result. Susceptibility requires Kirby-Bauer or MIC testing interpreted against breakpoints.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern to remember is the identification ladder: **Gram stain first**, then shape and arrangement, then a quick enzyme test (catalase), then selective and differential media, then a confirmatory test (coagulase). Each step should cut the possibilities roughly in half, and no step should be run before the one that makes it interpretable. Separately, oxacillin resistance in S. aureus always means altered target (PBP2a from mecA), never simple beta-lactamase — which is exactly why beta-lactamase inhibitor combinations fail against MRSA.

scenarios.title: Case conference: an outbreak on the orthopedic floor
scenarios.intro: Your microbiology class is given a real-format outbreak worksheet. Over `3 weeks`, six patients on one orthopedic unit developed watery diarrhea. Four had received cefazolin or ciprofloxacin in the prior `10 days`. Stool testing is positive for toxigenic *Clostridioides difficile* in five of them. You are asked to reason through the epidemiology the way an infection preventionist would.

steps.prompt: First, classify what you are looking at. Baseline on this unit is about one case every `3 months`. Six cases in `3 weeks` is best described as:

choices.text: An epidemic (outbreak) — more cases than expected for this place and time
choices.feedback: Correct. Epidemic simply means an excess over the expected baseline in a defined population; scale can be one hospital unit.

choices.text: Endemic disease, since C. difficile is always present in hospitals
choices.feedback: Endemic describes a constant background rate. The point of an outbreak investigation is that the rate has exceeded that background, which is what six cases in three weeks does.

choices.text: A pandemic, because C. difficile occurs worldwide
choices.feedback: Pandemic means an epidemic crossing countries or continents. A single hospital unit does not meet that definition no matter how widely the organism is distributed.

choices.text: Sporadic cases, since each patient was admitted separately
choices.feedback: Sporadic means occasional and unconnected. Clustering in time, place and antibiotic exposure argues strongly against chance.

steps.prompt: Four of six patients had recent cefazolin or ciprofloxacin. Explain the mechanism linking antibiotics to *C. difficile* disease.

choices.text: Broad-spectrum antibiotics eliminate competing colonic flora, allowing resistant C. difficile to overgrow and release toxins A and B
choices.feedback: Exactly. This is superinfection and it is an ecological effect, not direct drug toxicity. Losing microbial antagonism is what opens the niche.

choices.text: The antibiotics directly injure the colonic mucosa, producing diarrhea
choices.feedback: Direct mucosal toxicity can cause mild diarrhea, but it does not produce toxin-positive stool or pseudomembranes. The disease here is caused by an organism, not the drug.

choices.text: The antibiotics caused a mutation converting normal E. coli into C. difficile
choices.feedback: Species do not convert into one another. Antibiotics select among organisms already present; they cannot rewrite one genus into another.

choices.text: The antibiotics triggered an IgE-mediated allergic colitis
choices.feedback: Allergy presents with rash, urticaria or anaphylaxis, not toxin-positive watery stool. Serology and stool toxin testing separate these easily.

steps.prompt: Staff report using alcohol hand rub between every patient, and rooms are wiped with a quaternary ammonium disinfectant. What is the flaw?

choices.text: Neither alcohol nor quats are sporicidal; handwashing with soap and water plus a bleach-based agent is required
choices.feedback: Correct, and this is the most common real-world failure. Alcohol leaves spores viable on hands and quats leave them viable on surfaces, so transmission continues despite good compliance.

choices.text: Nothing is wrong; alcohol is the gold standard for all organisms
choices.feedback: Alcohol is excellent for vegetative bacteria and enveloped viruses, but endospores and naked viruses such as norovirus survive it entirely. The exception is the whole point here.

choices.text: The problem is that staff wash hands too frequently, damaging skin barrier
choices.feedback: Skin breakdown is a real occupational issue but it is not what drives an outbreak. The failure here is that the agents used do not kill the organism's spore form.

choices.text: Quats should be replaced with 70% alcohol on surfaces
choices.feedback: That swaps one non-sporicidal agent for another. A sporicidal agent such as a sodium hypochlorite solution is what the situation requires.

steps.prompt: You are asked to name the single most important upstream intervention to prevent the next cluster.

choices.text: Antibiotic stewardship — narrower, shorter, indication-driven antibiotic use
choices.feedback: Correct. Contact precautions and bleach interrupt transmission, but stewardship removes the condition that makes patients susceptible in the first place.

choices.text: Prophylactic oral vancomycin for every orthopedic admission
choices.feedback: This adds antibiotic pressure to a problem caused by antibiotic pressure, and it drives vancomycin resistance. Prophylaxis is not an outbreak control measure here.

choices.text: Testing every patient on admission and treating all colonized patients
choices.feedback: Asymptomatic colonization is common and treating it does not reduce disease; it selects resistance and can itself disturb flora further. Testing is for symptomatic patients.

choices.text: Installing UV lamps in hallways
choices.feedback: UV does not penetrate surfaces, shadows or soil, and hallway air is not the transmission route. Whole-room UV as an adjunct to terminal cleaning is a different, more targeted use.

steps.prompt: Final question on the worksheet: using the chain of infection, name which link each control measure breaks.

choices.text: Bleach cleaning breaks transmission; private room and gowns break portal of exit and transmission; stewardship protects the susceptible host
choices.feedback: Well reasoned. Mapping each control to a link is how infection preventionists check that a bundle actually covers the chain rather than piling on redundant measures.

choices.text: All measures break the 'infectious agent' link because they reduce organisms
choices.feedback: Too coarse. The agent link is broken only by eliminating the organism at its source; environmental and behavioral controls act on transmission, exit and host susceptibility.

choices.text: None of these apply because C. difficile is endogenous flora
choices.feedback: C. difficile is carried by a minority of adults but hospital outbreaks are overwhelmingly transmitted from the environment and staff hands, so every link is actionable.

scenarios.debrief: Two patterns worth keeping. First, an outbreak is defined relative to a baseline, not by an absolute number — six cases is an epidemic on a unit that normally sees four a year. Second, control measures should be mapped to specific links in the chain of infection so you can see what is actually covered: sporicidal cleaning and handwashing attack transmission, isolation attacks the portal of exit, and antibiotic stewardship is the only measure that reduces host susceptibility. When alcohol-based products are failing, ask whether the organism has a spore form or a naked capsid — those two properties explain nearly every disinfection failure you will meet.
